questions.text: Define a topological space and state the topology axioms.
Define a limit point of a set A in a topological space X.
State and prove the properties of closed sets: (i) the empty set and X are closed; (ii) any intersection of closed sets is closed; (iii) a finite union of closed sets is closed.

solution.finalAnswer: See the full proof on the Closure and Limit Points topic page (via De Morgan's laws).

questions.text: Let τ be the class of all subsets of X whose complements are finite, together with ∅. Show that τ is a topology on X (the cofinite topology).
questions.originalText: Let τ be the class of all subsets of X whose complements are finite, together with ∅. Show that τ is a topology on X.

solution.hint: Check each axiom directly, using that a finite union of finite sets is finite.
solution.steps: **Axiom 1:** $X\setminus X=\emptyset$ is finite, so $X\in\tau$; and $\emptyset\in\tau$ by definition. **Axiom 2 (unions):** for $\{U_i\}\subseteq\tau$ (each with finite complement, ignoring the trivial $\emptyset$ members), $X\setminus\bigcup_i U_i = \bigcap_i(X\setminus U_i)$, an intersection of finite sets, hence finite (intersecting with any one finite set already bounds the size) — so $\bigcup_i U_i\in\tau$. **Axiom 3 (finite intersections):** for $U_1,\dots,U_n\in\tau$, $X\setminus\bigcap_{k=1}^nU_k = \bigcup_{k=1}^n(X\setminus U_k)$, a finite union of finite sets, hence finite — so $\bigcap_{k=1}^n U_k\in\tau$.
solution.finalAnswer: All three topology axioms hold, so τ (the cofinite topology) is indeed a topology on X.
solution.examReady: Verify via De Morgan: complements of unions/intersections of members of τ turn into intersections/unions of finite sets, which stay finite — confirming all three axioms.
solution.commonMistakes: Forgetting to handle the $\emptyset$ member of $\tau$ separately (its complement $X$ need not be finite) when checking unions/intersections.

questions.text: In a topology τ = {X, ∅, {a}, {c,d}, {a,c,d}, {b,c,d,e}} on X = {a,b,c,d,e}, is b a limit point of A = {a,c}? Justify.
questions.originalText: In a topology τ = {X, ∅, {a}, {c,d}, {a,c,d}, {b,c,d,e}} on X = {a,b,c,d,e}, which is not discrete or indiscrete, are a, c limit points of A? Justify. [Interpreted here for A={a,c}, testing point b, matching the standard version of this recurring exam question.]

solution.hint: Find the smallest open set containing the test point, and check whether it meets A elsewhere.
solution.steps: **Is $b$ a limit point of $A=\{a,c\}$?** The open sets containing $b$ are $\{b,c,d,e\}$ and $X$; the smallest is $\{b,c,d,e\}$, which contains $c\in A$ (and $c\ne b$). So **yes**, $b$ is a limit point of $A$. **Is $a$ a limit point of $A$?** The smallest open set containing $a$ is $\{a\}$ itself, which contains no point of $A$ other than $a$. So **no**, $a$ is not a limit point of $A$ (it's an isolated point of $A$ within this topology). **Is $c$ a limit point of $A$?** The smallest open set containing $c$ is $\{c,d\}$, which contains no point of $A\setminus\{c\}$ (since $a\notin\{c,d\}$). So **no**, $c$ is not a limit point of $A$ either.
solution.finalAnswer: b IS a limit point of A = {a,c}; a and c are NOT limit points of A.
solution.examReady: Always test using the smallest open set containing the point in question — for finite topologies this makes the check immediate.
solution.commonMistakes: Testing with a larger open set (e.g. X itself) instead of the smallest one containing the point, which can wrongly suggest a point is a limit point.

questions.text: Is A = {1, 1/2, 1/3, ...} dense in R (with the usual topology)? Prove your answer.
questions.originalText: Let A = {1, ½, ⅓, …} ⊂ ℝ (usual topology). Is A dense in ℝ? Prove your answer.

solution.hint: Compute the closure of A directly: find all its limit points.
solution.steps: $A$'s only limit point is $0$ (the terms $1/n\to0$, and no other real number has points of $A$ arbitrarily close to it, since $A$'s points are isolated from each other away from $0$). So $\bar A = A\cup\{0\}$. Since $\bar A \ne \mathbb R$ (e.g. $2\notin\bar A$), $A$ is not dense.
solution.finalAnswer: A is NOT dense in R; its closure is A ∪ {0}, far from all of R.
solution.examReady: $\bar A=A\cup\{0\}\ne\mathbb R$, so $A$ fails the definition of density (\bar A=\mathbb R).
solution.commonMistakes: Confusing “accumulates somewhere” with “dense everywhere” — density requires the closure to be the *entire* space, not just to have a limit point.

questions.text: Show that the union of two topologies need not be a topology.
questions.originalText: Show the union of topologies need not be a topology.

solution.finalAnswer: See the Difficult worked example (τ₁={X,∅,{a}}, τ₂={X,∅,{b}} on X={a,b,c}) on the Topological Spaces topic page — their union fails axiom 2 since {a}∪{b}={a,b} is missing.

questions.text: Prove: G is open if and only if G is a neighbourhood of each of its points.
questions.originalText: Prove: G is open iff G is a neighbourhood of each of its points.

solution.hint: A neighbourhood of p is any set containing an open set that contains p.
solution.steps: ($\Rightarrow$) If $G$ is open, then $G$ itself is an open set containing $p$ for every $p\in G$, so $G$ is (trivially) a neighbourhood of each of its points. ($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $G$ is a neighbourhood of each $p\in G$: for each such $p$, there's an open $U_p$ with $p\in U_p\subseteq G$. Then $G = \bigcup_{p\in G} U_p$ (each $p$ is in its own $U_p$, and every $U_p\subseteq G$), a union of open sets, hence open.
solution.finalAnswer: Both directions verified — G is open iff it is a neighbourhood of every one of its points.
solution.commonMistakes: In the reverse direction, forgetting to actually exhibit G as a union of the open sets U_p, rather than just asserting openness.
